newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Politics block anti-Taleban push on Afghan capital.
newsitem.headline: Politics block anti-Taleban push on Afghan capital.

text.p: Forces loyal to the former Afghan government are far from ousting their Taleban foe from the capital Kabul despite a rain of rockets and shells on the radical Islamic militia in recent days.

The two-year-old Taleban, which has seized control of over two-thirds of the country, has put up stiff resistance against assaults north of Kabul. The city is a politically vital prize in the battle to control the fractious country of 17 million.

The air shook and the horizon was a cloud of dust and smoke on Thursday as forces under the command of ex-government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood tried for a third time to push the Taleban off the strategic heights 25 to 30 km (15 to 19 miles) north of Kabul.

But Masood's camp, comprising former government forces allied to those of the northern Uzbek leader, General Abdul Rashid Dostum, said the push gained only "a few hundred metres" and neither of two passes.

After putting the Taleban on the run only days after the fundamentalist group seized Kabul at the end of September, Ahmad Shah Masood -- probably the ablest mujahedin commander during the 1979 Soviet invasion -- is stuck.
The ground, and some of the fighters' poor knowledge of it, does not help.
Below the De Sabz pass, about 30 km (19 miles) north of Kabul, the anti-Taleban alliance's troops and armour are ranged out in mostly desert terrain with little cover.
Soldiers lie in shallow trenches scratched from the sand while highly visible armoured vehicles are a boon for enemy spotters from the peaks above.
When not fighting, combatants on both sides tune into their opponents' field radios and bawl unprintable insults at each other.
A Masood official hinted at difficulties in the field inside the alliance.
"The Jumbish-i-Milli (Dostum) troops don't know the area very well, it's a problem," the official said.
In the treacherous world of Afghan politics, observers have also wondered how long the alliance will actually stick.

Masood and Dostum were until recently bitter enemies, fighting over the Salang highway in 1994. Earlier this month, Dostum took several days before throwing in his lot with Masood, anxious only to find the best way of protecting the autonomy of six northern provinces under his control.
"We must take Kabul as this will be a sign that we are serious," said a senior official inside the alliance on Thursday.

The anti-Taleban alliance is looking to the recapture of Kabul to touch off revolts against the Taleban elsewhere in Afghanistan, particularly in the mainly ethnic Tajik city of Herat in the west which the largely Pashtun Taleban seized last year.

"Masood's underground are active at night (in Kabul), waiting for a revolt after which there will be a big change in Afghanistan," said Amir Mohammad, a jovial Jumbish commander wearing a raffish red scarf near the frontline on Thursday.
But he added: "As you can hear and see, this kind of fighting (artillery and rocket assaults) is not so strong, there are serious political considerations."

The former Afghan government is drawn over a barrel by its stated desire on the one hand to avoid massive bloodshed in a fight for the capital, while on the other, time for a decisive push is running out as winter approaches.
Long, drawn out fighting and attacks such as the bombing of Kabul with warplanes on Thursday, which killed three children, also endanger any sympathy for the former government.

"We want peace in Afghanistan, there should be negotiations," said 60-year-old Abdur Rahman, on his way back from the bazaar in the village of Qarabagh near the front line, cursing war for driving up food prices.
